items.title: Charles Tolliver interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, May 6, 2021 [interview 1 of 2]
items.q: before he would bring in horns and then so when you showed up, you know, the way to interpret it was already there you know, and so that approach stayed with me and I was grateful to have had an opportunity to basically from time to time perform with Andrew

ctx.x: No not instruction, just observing how he allowed the people that he had gathered for whatever, a recording or performances, to interpret the music without being dogmatic as

to how he wanted it done. Yeah. But he always chose rhythm section guys that really helped set it up because they knew, you know, how he probably wanted things to go. And of course I think he probably always worked things out with his rhythm section before he would bring in horns and then so when you showed up, you know, the way to interpret it was already there you know, and so that approach stayed with me and I was grateful to have had an opportunity to basically from time to time perform with Andrew at the…
Is it possible for you to describe the thought process that is occurring when you’re improvising?

items.title: Tolliver interviewed by Monk Rowe, 2021
items.q: once I started playing with Andrew and recording with him

ctx.x: Well you know I wouldn’t be where I am today, you know, in this art form, had it not been for Jackie McLean. That’s what I’m talking about, that lucky break you know. And my first, my debut recording with him, as you know, Jackie was a dye-in-the-wool, you know, bebopper. But that was, I came in during that generational shift just as you know the freer forms were being used. I mean he was already, he had already done “Destination Out” and a couple of other things which portend that he, you know, he wasn’t just…

thing. And he wanted something a little bit different. And so you know like half of that recording is bebop and half of it is what you are talking about. And from that experience I think is where I started to do those sorts of things that this person observed in my work. But I think Andrew Hill is the one who really, once I started playing with Andrew and recording with him, you know, that sort of thing really became also a part of my delivery process.

It just occurred to me that 1964 is a significant year for you, it was also the Civil Rights Bill of 1964, and if you extrapolate on that, was the situation socially and politically at that time, do you feel it affected the change in jazz that you’re describing?
